justification: run-code is green (26 blocks, 13 executed, exit 0). I re-derived or checked every load-bearing claim against a primary source I opened myself: LinkedList<T> class docs (doubly linked; 'insertion and removal are O(1) operations', quoted verbatim and matches; multithreaded-read-only wording matches), LinkedList<T>.Find docs ('This method performs a linear search; therefore, this method is an O(n) operation', quoted and matches), List<T>.Insert docs ('This method is an O(n) operation', matches), List<T>.RemoveAt docs ('O(n) operation, where n is (Count - index)', matches the article's O(n - index)), LinkedListNode<T>.Previous docs (returns null when the node is First, matches the article's demo output), and the dotnet/runtime LinkedList.cs source plus the class remarks (confirmed: 'This LinkedList is a doubly-Linked circular list', a version field that throws InvalidOperationException on a version mismatch in the enumerator - matches the article's throws=InvalidOperationException block). Ulrich Drepper's memory paper was opened and both quoted fragments ('cannot cross page boundaries', 'do not recognize non-linear access patterns') are exact substrings of the real text. The programs are correct: I read every implementation (SinglyLinkedList, the sentinel-based DoublyLinkedList, Reverse, LruCache, NaiveLruCache) and traced them by hand; the RemoveFirst/_tail bug in the first exercise is real and the explanation is exactly right; the sentinel InsertBefore/Remove rewiring is correct; the LRU cache's O(1) argument is correct because the node reference always comes from the dictionary. Against the three best-ranking pages for this kind of query that I read in full (GeeksforGeeks' linked-list hub, Programiz's linked-list page, Wikipedia's Linked list article - I could not run a live search this session because the environment's WebSearch quota was already exhausted, and Bing/DuckDuckGo results fetched via WebFetch would not render real organic results, so I cannot certify these are literally today's top-3 for the literal string 'linked list explained', but they are the well-established top-ranking pages for this topic and I read all three rather than assuming), this article is substantially deeper: none of the three has a single line of C#, none re-derives or measures memory overhead or seek cost, none builds a working LRU cache, none cites BCL source code or a systems paper, and none discusses the sentinel technique, node identity under 'swap values and delete the next node,' or the version-check-throw. On substance and rigor this is a 9-caliber article. It does not score there because of two binding-rule problems. First (caps the score at 7 by the rubric): the article's own explanation of its memory measurement is factually wrong. I independently reproduced the experiment on this machine (GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread around new int[0], new int[1], new int[1000], and new object()) and the array's fixed overhead is 24 bytes (16-byte object header + 8-byte length field on this 64-bit runtime: new int[0] allocates exactly 24 bytes, new int[1000] allocates exactly 4024 = 24 + 1000*4), not the 'four bytes of overhead' the article states. The final displayed ratio (4.0 bytes/element) is still correct - 24 bytes spread over a million elements rounds away at one decimal place - but the sentence that explains why is simply the wrong number, not a rounding simplification. Second: two of the article's quoted fragments are not verbatim, despite being presented in quotation marks as if they were (hard rule 1 explicitly lists quotes among things that must never be fabricated). Both are listed below. Given one confirmed factual error and a second, independent sourcing-integrity problem, I am not scoring at the 7.0 ceiling but a little under it.

issues.location: "Two things worth measuring before you decide" / "What a node costs beyond its value", the sentence immediately after the id=memory output block: "The array holds four bytes of overhead across the whole 4 MB block, so it rounds to exactly 4.0 bytes per `int`."
issues.problem: Factually wrong. I measured this directly on the same toolchain (dotnet run, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread): new int[0] allocates 24 bytes, new int[1] allocates 32 bytes, and new int[1000] allocates 4024 bytes (= 24 + 1000*4). The array's fixed overhead - object header plus the stored Length - is 24 bytes on this 64-bit runtime, not four. 'Four bytes' is actually sizeof(int), the per-element payload, not the object's overhead; the sentence conflates the two. The final measured ratio (4.0 bytes/element) is still correct only because 24 bytes spread over 1,000,000 elements rounds to nothing at one decimal place - the explanation, not the headline number, is wrong. Per the critic rubric, a single factual error caps this score at 7.
issues.fixLooksLike: State the real fixed cost: e.g. 'A million-element array pays a small, fixed overhead once - the object header plus its stored length, about 24 bytes total on this runtime - and that fixed cost, spread across a million elements, disappears at one decimal place; what is left is just the four bytes each int itself occupies.' If a specific byte count is kept in prose, measure it the same way the rest of the section does (a GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread delta around new int[0]) rather than asserting a number that was not run.

issues.location: "What .NET actually ships: LinkedList<T>", the :::dotnet callout, sentence beginning 'Removing a node you have not stored anywhere...'/the paragraph before it: `nodes "can be removed and reinserted... which results in no additional heap allocations."` — and "What each operation costs, and under what assumption", first paragraph: `An array's length "cannot change for the lifetime of the instance"`
issues.problem: Both are presented as direct quotations (quotation marks, no paraphrase signal) but neither is verbatim. The actual LinkedList<T> class Remarks read: 'You can remove nodes and reinsert them, either in the same list or in another list, which results in no additional objects allocated on the heap.' The article's version rewrites the first clause from active to passive voice ('can be removed and reinserted' vs. 'You can remove nodes and reinsert them') and reorders the second ('no additional heap allocations' vs. 'no additional objects allocated on the heap') - the ellipsis marks an omission, but the surviving words on both sides of it do not match the source. Likewise the C# array reference actually says 'You can't change these values during the lifetime of the instance,' not 'cannot change for the lifetime of the instance' (the object of the sentence and the preposition are both changed). The substance of both claims is correct - I verified them against the same pages - but hard rule 1 lists quotes explicitly among things that must never be fabricated, and quotation marks around reworded text reads as verbatim when it is not.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the source exactly - 'You can remove nodes and reinsert them ... which results in no additional objects allocated on the heap' and 'You can't change these values during the lifetime of the instance' - or drop the quotation marks and state both claims in the article's own words, keeping the existing citations.

issues.location: "Two pointers per node..." section, DoublyLinkedList<T>.Node class (public sealed class Node(T value) with public mutable Next/Prev fields)
issues.problem: Node is a public nested type with public, freely mutable Next/Prev/Value fields, so any caller holding a node reference (as InsertBefore, Remove and AddLast all hand callers one) can rewrite another list's internal links directly and corrupt the sentinel invariant the rest of the section relies on. The real LinkedListNode<T> this section leads into only exposes Next/Previous as read-only properties (settable solely through list operations); the hand-rolled type is a step less safe than the BCL type it is modeling.
issues.fixLooksLike: Make Next/Prev get-only from outside the class (internal or private setters, public getters), or add one sentence acknowledging the simplification before LinkedList<T> is introduced with its read-only Previous/Next.
